h1: Power of Attorney & Medical Directives Lawyer El Paso, TX
intro: If you are in a hospital bed at University Medical Center and cannot speak for yourself, your family has no automatic authority over your care or your bank account. Attorney Robert Navar prepares the Texas documents that give the people you trust that authority before it is needed.
summary: A statutory durable power of attorney (Estates Code Ch. 752) lets your agent handle finances — bank accounts, bills, property, benefits — and stays effective if you become incapacitated. It must be signed before a notary.
A medical power of attorney and a directive to physicians (living will) under Health & Safety Code Ch. 166 name who makes medical decisions and state your wishes about life support.
A HIPAA release lets doctors share your records with family, and a declaration of guardian says who should — and who should not — be appointed if a guardianship ever becomes necessary.
These documents are included in our will packages or prepared on their own, flat fee quoted after a free consultation, with signings in English or Spanish. Call 915-503-1600.

sections.heading: Why Every Adult in El Paso Needs These Documents
paragraphs: Most people assume that if something happens to them, their spouse or adult child can simply step in. In Texas, that is only partly true. Hospitals have a default list of surrogate decision-makers for a patient who cannot communicate, but it covers only certain decisions, it does not resolve disputes between family members, and it does nothing for your finances. No bank will let your daughter pay your mortgage from your account, and no title company will let your husband sell your truck — unless they hold a power of attorney or a court order.

The court order is a guardianship, filed in the El Paso County probate courts at 500 E. San Antonio Ave. It takes months, requires an attorney ad litem, a doctor's certificate and a bond, and costs far more than the documents that would have avoided it — and a judge, not you, decides who is in charge.

A set of four or five signed documents prevents all of that. They are not just for the elderly: a 30-year-old soldier at Fort Bliss, a single parent, a business owner — anyone who could be in a crash on I-10 needs them alongside a will.

sections.heading: Durable Statutory Power of Attorney (Estates Code Chapter 752)
paragraphs: Texas publishes a statutory form in Estates Code § 752.051, and most banks and agencies in El Paso recognize it on sight. You name an agent and one or more alternates, then initial the powers you grant: real property, banking, insurance, retirement plans, government benefits, tax matters and digital assets. You can also grant or withhold the power to make gifts and to change beneficiary designations, which matters for keeping an agent from rewriting your estate plan.

The form lets you choose whether the power is effective immediately or only when a physician certifies you are incapacitated. Immediate powers are more practical — a "springing" power makes the bank evaluate a doctor's letter before honoring it — and most clients who trust their agent choose immediate. "Durable" means it survives your incapacity; it ends at your death, when the executor named in your will takes over. Under § 751.0021 the document must be signed before a notary, and we recommend recording it in the El Paso County property records if the agent may need to sign a deed.

sections.heading: Medical Power of Attorney, Living Will and HIPAA Release
paragraphs: The medical documents are governed by Health & Safety Code Chapter 166 and do different jobs. The medical power of attorney (§ 166.164 statutory form) names an agent to make any health-care decision you cannot make yourself — consent to surgery, choice of facility, hospice — and takes effect only while a physician has certified you incompetent. The directive to physicians, commonly called a living will (§ 166.033), is your own statement about life-sustaining treatment in a terminal or irreversible condition. The agent under the medical POA is bound by it.

Both may be signed before two qualified witnesses or a notary; we do both so no provider questions them. The HIPAA authorization is the piece families forget. Without it, a hospital's privacy office can refuse to tell your son in Dallas what is going on even though he is your medical agent. We draft one naming every family member you want in the loop.

sections.heading: Declaration of Guardian and Planning for Aging Parents
paragraphs: Even with good powers of attorney, a guardianship can become necessary — an agent dies, a facility refuses the POA, or a family member contests it. A declaration of guardian before need arises under Estates Code Chapter 1104 is your written instruction on who the court should appoint as guardian of your person and estate, and, just as important, who should be disqualified. Judges follow it unless the named person is unsuitable. For parents who want one child and not another in charge, this is the document that does it.

Aging-parent planning is a large part of our estate practice. The typical visit is a family group: the parent, two or three adult children, sometimes a grandchild who translates. We make sure the parent, not the children, is directing the plan, that the parent has capacity to sign, and that the documents are explained in the language the parent is most comfortable in. Where a parent is already declining, we can often still act if capacity is present at signing; if it is not, we talk honestly about guardianship and what comes after.

sections.heading: Revocation, Updates and Where to Keep the Originals
paragraphs: Every one of these documents can be revoked while you have capacity: by a written revocation, by a new document that replaces it, or — for a durable POA — by divorce, which automatically removes a former spouse as agent. Revocation only works if the people relying on the old document know about it, so we send written notice to the agent and to any bank or provider holding a copy.

Originals go in a safe, accessible place — not a safe-deposit box only you can open. Each agent gets a copy of the document naming them. Signings are at our office at 11860 Vista Del Sol Dr. #119 with a notary and two witnesses, in English or Spanish; for clients who cannot travel, we can sign at a hospital, nursing facility or home in El Paso County.

Fees are flat and quoted after a free consultation; the full set is typically bundled with a will in one of our estate-planning packages. This page is general information, not legal advice about your situation. Schedule an appointment or contact us to get started.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a durable power of attorney and a medical power of attorney?
faqs.a: The durable (financial) power of attorney under the Estates Code covers money and property. The medical power of attorney under the Health & Safety Code covers health-care decisions. They can name the same agent or different ones, and most people need both.

faqs.q: Does a power of attorney have to be notarized in Texas?
faqs.a: Yes for a durable power of attorney — Estates Code § 751.0021 requires it be signed before a notary. A medical power of attorney and a directive to physicians may be signed before either two witnesses or a notary; we use both so no hospital or bank questions them.

faqs.q: Can my family make medical decisions for me without these documents?
faqs.a: Sometimes, under Texas's surrogate decision-maker rules, but only for certain decisions and only if the family agrees. Disputes, financial matters and anything a facility is unsure about end up in a guardianship. The documents avoid that.

faqs.q: When does a power of attorney end?
faqs.a: At your death, when you revoke it, or when a court appoints a guardian and does not continue it. A durable power survives incapacity — that is the point of it. A former spouse's authority as agent ends automatically on divorce.

faqs.q: Can you prepare these for my parent who lives in El Paso but I live out of town?
faqs.a: Yes. Your parent is the client and must have capacity and want the documents, but we can hold the consultation with you by phone or video and schedule the signing at our office, a facility or their home, in English or Spanish.
